acko.summary: Acko is an insurance company with no branches and no agents.
lessons: In insurance, the claim is the product.
Cutting out middlemen lowers price, but you then pay to find customers yourself.
In regulated businesses, a strong product can still be slowed by rules on costs.

scenes.title: Who is it for?
scenes.prompt: Day 1. You are the new PM of Acko. An online-only insurance company that sells car, bike, health and life cover through its app, and tries to make claims fast and painless. Who do you build for first?
right: Young car owner: a 28-year-old in Bengaluru with a 2-year-old Baleno.

wrong.text: The weekend binge-watcher: a 27-year-old in Bengaluru who watches K-dramas, Indian originals and true crime on weekends.
Independent barber: works alone and rents a chair in Manchester.
Corporate recruiter: a talent acquisition manager at an IT services company hiring 200 engineers a quarter.
Budget first-time smartphone upgrader: a buyer in a tier-2 city looking at CMF phones around ₹15,000 to ₹19,000.
Health-focused home cook: someone who wants A2-style cow milk, desi ghee, fresh paneer and dahi made from fresh milk.
Family on JioAirFiber: a family in Jaipur that switched from cable TV to AirFiber.

scenes.win: Right. A 28-year-old in Bengaluru with a 2-year-old Baleno. They want: cheapest renewal; easy claims.
scenes.lose: You built for the wrong crowd. They try Acko once and leave. Hint: Acko's real users want things like "cheapest renewal".

scenes.title: What hurts?
scenes.prompt: You sit with a few of these users. Which problem do they keep bringing up?
right: Insurance bought through dealers and agents costs more.

wrong.text: Phones get slow and stop getting updates after a few years.
Smartphones were too expensive for most Indians.
English tests like IELTS are costly and need a test centre.
Branded fashion is expensive.
Fake profiles make online dating unsafe.
Hard to keep in touch with old colleagues.

scenes.win: Yes. Acko solves it like this: Direct online sales with lower prices.
scenes.lose: You fixed a problem these users rarely have. Hint: one thing that frustrates them is "dealer-pushed insurance is costly".

scenes.title: Build the core
scenes.prompt: You can build one thing first. Which feature becomes the heart of Acko?
right: Instant car and bike insurance: quote and buy in minutes using the vehicle number.

wrong.text: Business loans: offers loans of ₹50,000 to ₹5 lakh from partner NBFCs, repaid in daily instalments.
Price Prediction: estimates how Advance fares will rise, nudging people to book early.
Multi-currency account: hold and convert 40+ currencies, with local bank details in several of them.
udaanCapital credit: buy now, pay later for retailers, through lending partners.
Buyer and seller protection: refunds for undelivered items and seller cover.
AI personalisation: shows content for your favourite teams, leagues and players.

scenes.win: Good call. Motor is Acko's main business and entry point.
scenes.lose: Users shrug. That feature belongs to a different kind of product. Hint: Acko's promise is "Cheaper insurance bought in minutes, with fast app-based claims and no agent calling you."

scenes.title: Make money
scenes.prompt: Investors ask: where will most of Acko's money come from?
right: Motor insurance premiums: car and bike cover, the biggest line.

wrong.text: Business subscriptions: monthly fees for the Business Toolkit, Ember accounting and other add-ons.
Commission from cinemas and organisers: a share of ticket value, higher for events than movies.
Retail trading fees: fees and spreads on buys and sells, highest in the simple app.
Broadband and mobile: about 6.6 million broadband and 3.7 million mobile customers.
Interest income: interest on client money and margin funding.
Advertising: brands pay for placement and campaigns on the site.

scenes.win: That's it. Acko is the insurer, so it keeps the premium and pays claims.
scenes.lose: Revenue barely moves, and runway shrinks. Hint, look at how Acko prices things: "Prices shown instantly on the site based on vehicle, age and cover."

scenes.title: Pick the north star
scenes.prompt: The team needs one number to chase every week. Which north star fits Acko?
right: Claims settled within the promised time with a positive customer rating, per month

wrong.text: Weekly active merchants who record at least one transaction
Orders delivered on time and complete per week (in 15 minutes or less, with no missing or damaged items)
Monthly active accounts that complete at least one branded checkout
Monthly hours of listening per active user
Number of purchases repaid on time by active users each month
Number of buyers who make a repeat purchase within 12 months

scenes.win: Yes. A claim is the moment insurance proves its worth.
scenes.lose: The team chases the wrong number and the product drifts. Hint: a good north star counts the moment a Acko user gets real value.

scenes.title: Build the KPI tree
scenes.prompt: Your north star is "Claims settled within the promised time with a positive customer rating, per month". Pick all 3 numbers that directly drive it.
right: Claim speed
Claim fairness
Policies in force

wrong.text: Cross-product use
App ecosystem health
Cost per million tokens served
Paid seat retention
Match rate
Fans in working use

scenes.win: Your tree holds. Claim speed: how fast claims are paid. Claim fairness: customers feel treated well. Policies in force: active customers.
scenes.lose: Your tree has the wrong branches, so the team works on numbers that don't move the goal. Hint: "Claim speed" is one real driver.

scenes.title: Grow
scenes.prompt: Time to grow. Pick the 2 ways Acko really gets new users.
right: Google search for car insurance
Cheeky TV and digital ads

wrong.text: Celebrity and influencer marketing
Low introductory InstaHelp prices
Corporate deals through myBiz
Word of mouth and WhatsApp shares
TV ads with celebrities
Paid ads for QuickTV dramas on Meta, YouTube and its own apps

scenes.win: That's how Acko grows. What brings people back: yearly motor and health renewals
scenes.lose: You spend a lot and users don't come. Hint: what keeps Acko users coming back is "yearly motor and health renewals"

scenes.win: Right. Listed digital-first insurer that sells mainly through agents and partners. How Acko differs: Acko sells mostly direct; Digit uses agents and is profitable at larger scale.
scenes.lose: You watched the wrong company, and the real rival takes your users. Hint, they are described as: "Listed digital-first insurer that sells mainly through agents and partners."

wrong.text: Revenue: About £1.7 billion (year to March 2026)

Guidance: Raised four quarters in a row

scenes.win: Correct. Source: Acko General Insurance via Inc42.
scenes.lose: That number belongs to another product. Hint: look for the one that fits Acko's size and model: think of ₹100 of premium earned.

scenes.title: Set a guardrail
scenes.prompt: You push hard on "Claims settled within the promised time with a positive customer rating, per month". Which number must NOT get worse while you do?
right: Claims ratio

wrong.text: Customer support contacts per 1,000 tickets
Cash burn per month
Gross margin per car

scenes.title: Read the reviews
scenes.prompt: You open the app store reviews. Which complaint do Acko users really make?
right: Health claims rejected or partly paid

wrong.text: Feeling invisible without paying
Sponsored results crowd out organic products
Scam messages and fake job offers, often from foreign numbers
Concerns about not notifying others in the call
Hard to get the exact same character across images

scenes.win: Yes. Other complaints you'll see: slow customer support for complex claims; renewal premiums rise.
scenes.lose: That complaint comes from a different product's users. Hint: Acko users get frustrated by things like "garage visits for claims"

scenes.title: Crisis
scenes.prompt: Trouble. Users feel claims are unfairly cut What do you ship?
right: Clear 'why this was deducted' breakdown for every claim

wrong.text: Show Premium users a monthly 'value report' of ads skipped, songs downloaded and audiobook hours used.
Feed control panel with topic sliders
Verified-fan lottery for mega concerts instead of first-come queues
Clear download limits page with a meter and options to buy more downloads
India cricket-adjacent content and a low-priced ad plan bundled with telecoms.
In hindsight: launch dark stores only in a few dense Bengaluru areas first

scenes.win: Shipped. Higher trust and fewer complaints You track it with: claim complaints per 10,000 claims.
scenes.lose: The fix misses the problem and complaints grow. Hint: the right fix would move "claim complaints per 10,000 claims".

agoda.summary: Agoda is a travel app where you book hotels, homes, flights and activities, mostly for trips in Asia.
lessons: Focus can beat size. Agoda wins in Asia by knowing local hotels, payments and languages better than global rivals.
Winning on price brings users, but trust keeps them.
Inside a group, sister brands can cover different regions instead of fighting each other.

scenes.title: Who is it for?
scenes.prompt: Day 1. You are the new PM of Agoda. An Asia-focused travel booking app, owned by Booking Holdings, known for cheap hotel deals across Asia. Who do you build for first?
right: Indian traveller going to Southeast Asia: a 28-year-old from Mumbai planning a Thailand or Bali trip with friends.

wrong.text: Long-term investor: a 40-year-old engineer who buys stocks and funds and holds for years.
Urban professional who orders food often: a 29-year-old in Bengaluru or Hyderabad who orders dinner 3 to 4 times a week.
Student applying to college: an 18-year-old who needs to submit Class 10 and 12 marksheets.
Budget family shopper: buys kids' clothes, home items and basics.
Bank card business head: wants more spending on the bank's cards.
Life sciences researcher: a biologist at an Indian institute who uses AlphaFold to understand a protein before running lab tests.

scenes.win: Right. A 28-year-old from Mumbai planning a Thailand or Bali trip with friends. They want: lowest hotel price; Pay in rupees with UPI or card.
scenes.lose: You built for the wrong crowd. They try Agoda once and leave. Hint: Agoda's real users want things like "lowest hotel price".

scenes.title: What hurts?
scenes.prompt: You sit with a few of these users. Which problem do they keep bringing up?
right: Hotels across Asia are hard to compare in one place.

wrong.text: AI assistants are expensive for many users in India and other markets.
Writing repetitive code, tests and boilerplate takes a lot of time.
Need a training plan without a coach.
Not knowing which seats are left.
Ideas die in documents because building a prototype takes weeks.
Messy staff rotas and commission.

scenes.win: Yes. Agoda solves it like this: Large Asian supply, including small hotels and homes, with reviews and maps.
scenes.lose: You fixed a problem these users rarely have. Hint: one thing that frustrates them is "taxes and fees added at the end".

scenes.title: Build the core
scenes.prompt: You can build one thing first. Which feature becomes the heart of Agoda?
right: Hotel and home search with deals: shows rooms with discount tags, ratings and photos.

wrong.text: Everywhere search: lists cheapest destinations from your airport.
Add-on essentials: curd, paneer, ghee, eggs, bread, fruit, vegetables and more on the same drop.
Captain subscription (zero commission): drivers pay a fixed fee per day or per ride rather than a percentage.
Glyph Interface and Glyph Matrix: LED lights on the back (a small dot display on Phone 3) that show calls, charging, timers and small toys.
S1 scooter range: s1 Pro, S1 Air and S1 X with different batteries and prices.
Affordability (EMI and offers) engine: shows and applies bank and brand EMI and cashback offers at checkout.

scenes.win: Good call. Price is the main reason users pick Agoda.
scenes.lose: Users shrug. That feature belongs to a different kind of product. Hint: Agoda's promise is "The cheapest-looking deals for stays across Asia, in local languages and currencies, including small hotels and homes that global..."

scenes.title: Make money
scenes.prompt: Investors ask: where will most of Agoda's money come from?
right: Hotel and home bookings: commission or markup on prepaid stays.

wrong.text: Subscription (old model): monthly fees for car subscriptions, closed down before the collapse.
Late-shipping and quality fines: suppliers can be fined for delays or poor quality, though this is a small slice.
Partner revenue: shared fares when rides come through Uber or Lyft.
RazorpayX and payouts: fees per payout and for current account and payroll features.
Used-car sales: buys low, refurbishes, sells at a fixed price.
Sexual health: ED and premature ejaculation treatments, often personalised.

scenes.win: That's it. Agoda mostly uses a merchant model: guests pay Agoda upfront, and Agoda pays the hotel later at a lower price.
scenes.lose: Revenue barely moves, and runway shrinks. Hint, look at how Agoda prices things: "Free for travellers; prices include deals and show taxes at checkout."

airbnb.summary: Airbnb lets ordinary people rent out their flat, spare room or holiday home to travellers.
lessons: Trust is the real product in a marketplace of strangers: reviews, protection and support make it possible.
Changing fees moves money between hosts and guests.
Growth features like Pay Later can raise bookings and cancellations at the same time, so watch both.

scenes.title: Who is it for?
scenes.prompt: Day 1. You are the new PM of Airbnb. A global app where people book homes, rooms, experiences and services from local hosts instead of hotels. Who do you build for first?
right: Family or friends group: four to eight people who want one house with a kitchen for a week.

wrong.text: Young professional: 25 to 35, salaried, wants an everyday account that helps them budget.
Rate hunter: keeps money where interest is best and moves it often.
Busy middle manager: a manager with 30 meetings a week and 200 emails a day.
Young bachelor who cooks rarely: a 25-year-old in a PG or flat who wants quick protein without cleaning fish or chicken.
School student: a Class 6 to 10 student who used the app after school.
Freelancer with global clients: designer or developer in the UK or Europe who invoices clients in dollars and euros.

scenes.win: Right. Four to eight people who want one house with a kitchen for a week. They want: space and bedrooms for everyone; clear total price split per person.
scenes.lose: You built for the wrong crowd. They try Airbnb once and leave. Hint: Airbnb's real users want things like "space and bedrooms for everyone".

scenes.title: What hurts?
scenes.prompt: You sit with a few of these users. Which problem do they keep bringing up?
right: Hotels are cramped and expensive for groups and long stays.

wrong.text: No trusted place to learn about markets.
Awkward to ask friends for money.
Paying for many AI apps to get the best models is expensive.
Food is expensive, especially treats and fresh bakery items.
Card payments are expensive for recurring billing.
Shops struggle to find new customers online.

scenes.win: Yes. Airbnb solves it like this: Whole homes with kitchens and bedrooms, plus weekly and monthly discounts.
scenes.lose: You fixed a problem these users rarely have. Hint: one thing that frustrates them is "cleaning fees and long checkout chore lists".

scenes.title: Build the core
scenes.prompt: You can build one thing first. Which feature becomes the heart of Airbnb?
right: Search with total price and map: shows listings on a map with the full price including fees, and AI search in the US.

wrong.text: S1 scooter range: s1 Pro, S1 Air and S1 X with different batteries and prices.
Vidyapeeth and Pathshala centres: offline and hybrid classrooms in 353 locations.
Zero commission driver plan: drivers pay a daily or capped per-ride fee instead of a cut.
10-minute delivery: shows how many minutes delivery will take and delivers from a store about 2 km away.
Eyes-on driver assistance: hands-free assisted driving for consumer cars.
Performance marketing engine: thousands of ad clips tested on Instagram and YouTube.

scenes.win: Good call. Helps guests compare fairly and reduces the shock of fees at checkout.
scenes.lose: Users shrug. That feature belongs to a different kind of product. Hint: Airbnb's promise is "For guests: more space, a kitchen and a local feel, often cheaper than hotels for groups and families."

scenes.title: Make money
scenes.prompt: Investors ask: where will most of Airbnb's money come from?
right: Stay booking fees: about 15.5% host-only fee on most bookings.

wrong.text: Advertising: ads to the large base of users checking train status.
API: generate videos programmatically for personalised outreach and product videos.
Manufacturer and agency ads: carmakers pay for display ads.
Individual plans: plus ($8), Pro ($20, legacy) and Premium ($30) a month; new customers moved to an 'X Subscription' bundle after the SpaceX deal.
Service, parts and accessories: repairs, spares, extended warranty.
Usage-based charges: extra fees when users go beyond included model usage.

scenes.win: That's it. Airbnb earns a fee on every booking.
scenes.lose: Revenue barely moves, and runway shrinks. Hint, look at how Airbnb prices things: "Free to list and search. Most hosts pay about 15.5% of each booking. A direct booking link pilot cuts this to 6% or 10%. Guests see a total..."

airtel-thanks.summary: Airtel is India's second-largest mobile network.

wrong.text: The budget viewer on the ad plan: a student in Mexico City or London on the ad-supported plan.
Instagram home brand: a two-person team selling handmade candles from Jaipur, 300 orders a month.
Government job aspirant: a 23-year-old graduate preparing for SSC, banking or state exams while living with parents.
Worried public figure or parent: someone concerned about their face or their child's being used in fake videos.
Small-town shopper: buys from a local mobile shop.
Student or teacher: makes school projects, presentations and classroom posters.

scenes.win: Right. A family in Bengaluru or Pune that buys a full month of atta, rice, oil and cleaning supplies at once. They want: lowest total bill; big basket delivered in one trip.
scenes.lose: You built for the wrong crowd. They try BigBasket once and leave. Hint: BigBasket's real users want things like "lowest total bill".

scenes.title: What hurts?
scenes.prompt: You sit with a few of these users. Which problem do they keep bringing up?
right: Carrying heavy monthly groceries home

wrong.text: Cheap brands felt unreliable and unbranded.
Email threads are slow and messy for daily team talk.
Downloading apps from the web can be unsafe.
Opening a bank account is slow.
Getting bored of the same gym routine and quitting.
Small sellers could not afford marketplace commissions and penalties.

scenes.win: Yes. BigBasket solves it like this: Scheduled delivery of large baskets to the door.
scenes.lose: You fixed a problem these users rarely have. Hint: one thing that frustrates them is "slots not available on weekends".

scenes.title: Build the core
scenes.prompt: You can build one thing first. Which feature becomes the heart of BigBasket?
right: BB Now: fast delivery from dark stores, promised in 10 to 30 minutes.

wrong.text: Live tracking and support: map tracking, chat with Dasher, in-app refunds.
Text+ (US): second-number calling and texting app bought in 2026.
Sponsored listings: restaurants pay to rank higher.
Vision Pro and visionOS: eye and hand-controlled headset with spatial apps and immersive video.
Multi-store marketplace: browse and order from many local retailers in one app.
Bugbot and background agents: reviews pull requests and runs tasks in the cloud.

scenes.win: Good call. Defends against Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart, which were taking BigBasket's customers.
scenes.lose: Users shrug. That feature belongs to a different kind of product. Hint: BigBasket's promise is "A trusted Tata-owned grocery store with a wide range, good fresh produce and own brands, delivered fast or on your schedule."

scenes.title: Make money
scenes.prompt: Investors ask: where will most of BigBasket's money come from?
right: Product margin: difference between buying and selling price on groceries and household goods.

wrong.text: Merchant commissions: about 15% to 30% of the food price, depending on the plan.
Payment processing: about 3.3% plus $0.45 per US sale.
Advertising and other: sponsored ads from brands and enterprise software; $331 million in Q3 2026.
Ride fares: riders pay per trip, priced near or above Uber.
Grocery: margin on Hop and partner grocery orders.
Partner revenue: shared fares when rides come through Uber or Lyft.

scenes.win: That's it. BigBasket buys goods, owns the stock and sells at a markup.
scenes.lose: Revenue barely moves, and runway shrinks. Hint, look at how BigBasket prices things: "Free delivery above a minimum order value; delivery and small cart fees below it."

blinkit.summary: You open the Blinkit app, add milk, chips, a phone charger or a birthday gift, and pay.
lessons: Speed can be a product. Blinkit did not invent groceries online, it made them fast enough to change habits.
Fixed costs need volume. A dark store only makes money once it fills up with orders, so growth and profit are linked.
Ads can fund low prices. Brand ad money lets Blinkit keep customer fees low while still earning.

bolt.summary: Bolt is an app for booking a car ride, like Uber.
lessons: A low price is only a strategy if your costs are lower too; Bolt proves this by running lean.
In ride-hailing, supply comes first: a lower commission to drivers was Bolt's way into Uber's markets.

cred.summary: CRED is an app where you pay your credit card bills and get reward coins for it.
lessons: A free product can be a filter: CRED used credit card bill pay to collect only trusted, rich users, then sold them other things.
Brand can be a growth channel, but rewards that shrink over time slowly break the promise that brought users in.
Who your users are can matter more than how many: CRED's average UPI payment is almost three times PhonePe's.

scenes.title: Who is it for?
scenes.prompt: Day 1. You are the new PM of CRED. A members-only app for people with good credit scores that rewards them for paying credit card bills, then sells them loans, insurance and shopping. Who do you build for first?
right: Metro salaried professional with 3 cards: a 29-year-old in Bengaluru earning ₹25 lakh a year, using three credit cards for points.

wrong.text: Young gym regular: 18 to 28, trains 4 to 5 times a week and follows fitness creators.
The man who wants replies: a 31-year-old in Chicago who gets matches but waits for women to message.
Suburban family: parents in a US suburb who order dinner a few nights a week after work and kids' activities.
The full-time creator: a Hindi tech reviewer with 2 million subscribers who earns from ads, brand deals and memberships.
Product marketing manager: makes product demo and how-to videos at a software company.
US family switching from petrol: a suburban family buying a Model Y as the main car.

scenes.win: Right. A 29-year-old in Bengaluru earning ₹25 lakh a year, using three credit cards for points. They want: never miss a due date or pay late fees; track all cards in one place.
scenes.lose: You built for the wrong crowd. They try CRED once and leave. Hint: CRED's real users want things like "never miss a due date or pay late fees".

scenes.title: What hurts?
scenes.prompt: You sit with a few of these users. Which problem do they keep bringing up?
right: Missing a credit card due date leads to late fees and a lower credit score.

wrong.text: Free AI chat is limited or bland in big assistants like ChatGPT
Switching between apps to search and chat is slow.
Many people never try AI because it means a new app and an account.
People have only a few minutes at a time.
Picking a seat was not possible at agent shops.
Not knowing which dates are cheapest.

scenes.win: Yes. CRED solves it like this: CRED reads statements, sends reminders and lets you pay in a few taps.
scenes.lose: You fixed a problem these users rarely have. Hint: one thing that frustrates them is "coins feel worth very little".

scenes.title: Build the core
scenes.prompt: You can build one thing first. Which feature becomes the heart of CRED?
right: Credit card bill payment: Pay any card bill for free, with reminders and statement analysis.

wrong.text: Pension and pension finder: find and combine old pensions into one personal pension.
Kruti assistant (shut down): was a consumer AI agent to book cabs, order food and pay bills in Indian languages.
Fee-free foreign exchange: low-cost currency conversion within a monthly limit.
ChatGPT app and AI assistant: lets users plan and check train journeys inside ChatGPT and in the app.
Qwikcilver gift and prepaid cards: issues and manages gift cards and corporate cards.
Surprise Bags: bags of mixed surplus food at a fixed low price.

scenes.win: Good call. This is the hook. It brings trusted users back every month at no cost to them.
scenes.lose: Users shrug. That feature belongs to a different kind of product. Hint: CRED's promise is "For the user: one clean app to never miss a card bill, with rewards that feel like a premium club."

scenes.title: Make money
scenes.prompt: Investors ask: where will most of CRED's money come from?
right: Lending fees (CRED Cash and partners): partner banks and NBFCs pay CRED for loans it sources, and CRED's stake in Newtap Finance earns interest.

wrong.text: Partnership value: now mainly a technology asset inside Lloyds rather than a standalone business.
Partnerships: deals with big chains and brands.
Interest on balances and crypto: interest on money held and spreads on crypto trades.
Ola group services: Ola, Ola Electric and related firms buy computing and AI services; exact share not public.
PB Partners: commission on policies sold by local agents, shared with those agents.
Enterprise: enterprise Pro and Max seats for companies like PayPal and Ramp.

scenes.win: That's it. CRED gives bill payment away for free to attract people with good credit, then makes money by selling them loans, insurance, products and brand offers.
scenes.lose: Revenue barely moves, and runway shrinks. Hint, look at how CRED prices things: "Card bill payment via UPI or bank is free for members."

scenes.title: Pick the north star
scenes.prompt: The team needs one number to chase every week. Which north star fits CRED?

wrong.text: Monthly active users who spend and repay on time
Total paid subscriptions active on the platform
Number of purchases repaid on time by active users each month
Monthly active Sparks members who shop with M&S in more than one category
Value of payments successfully collected on time for businesses each month
Paid members who wear the ring at least 5 nights a week

scenes.win: Yes. It shows members trust CRED with real money every month.
scenes.lose: The team chases the wrong number and the product drifts. Hint: a good north star counts the moment a CRED user gets real value.

scenes.title: Build the KPI tree

scenes.win: Your tree holds. New qualified members: people above the credit score bar who join and add a card. Payment frequency: how often members pay through CRED each month (14.4 times in FY25). Products per member: 45% of active members use three or more CRED products.
scenes.lose: Your tree has the wrong branches, so the team works on numbers that don't move the goal. Hint: "New qualified members" is one real driver.

scenes.win: That's how CRED grows. What brings people back: monthly card bill due dates
scenes.lose: You spend a lot and users don't come. Hint: what keeps CRED users coming back is "monthly card bill due dates"

cult-fit.summary: Cult.fit is a gym membership you buy in an app.
lessons: Fitness products sell on hope but renew on habit.
Mixing owned and franchise supply lets you grow fast, but you must guard quality where you have less control.
A physical business lives on utilisation.

scenes.title: Who is it for?
scenes.prompt: Day 1. You are the new PM of Cult.fit. One membership for group workout classes, gyms and home workouts across Indian cities. Who do you build for first?
right: Young metro professional: 25 to 32, works in Bengaluru or Gurugram, gets bored of the same gym routine.

wrong.text: The game marketer: a marketing lead at a game studio who wants players to try a new title.
Brand marketer: works at a UK retailer and wants to reach young shoppers.
Gen Z vintage lover: 18 to 24, wants unique Y2K and vintage pieces.
School student: a Class 6 to 10 student who used the app after school.
Student applying to college: an 18-year-old who needs to submit Class 10 and 12 marksheets.
Family weekend orderer: parent in a UK town who orders a Friday night takeaway.

scenes.win: Right. 25 to 32, works in Bengaluru or Gurugram, gets bored of the same gym routine. They want: stay fit with fun group classes; work out near home on weekdays and near office on some days.
scenes.lose: You built for the wrong crowd. They try Cult.fit once and leave. Hint: Cult.fit's real users want things like "stay fit with fun group classes".

scenes.title: What hurts?
scenes.prompt: You sit with a few of these users. Which problem do they keep bringing up?
right: Getting bored of the same gym routine and quitting.

wrong.text: Scooters that do not get better over time
Travellers want the lowest price.
AI chatbots make things up and do not show where facts came from.
Sending money abroad is slow and expensive.
Small developers cannot build global payment and distribution systems.
Keeping up with trending edits is hard.

scenes.win: Yes. Cult.fit solves it like this: Many class formats in one pass, so the workout changes every day.
scenes.lose: You fixed a problem these users rarely have. Hint: one thing that frustrates them is "evening slots fill up fast".

scenes.title: Build the core
scenes.prompt: You can build one thing first. Which feature becomes the heart of Cult.fit?
right: cultpass ELITE: unlimited classes and gym access across all Cult centres in a city.

wrong.text: Courses and programmes: multi-day courses on topics like anxiety, sleep and self-esteem.
AI Mode: a chat-style search tab with follow-ups, deep research and agent features like booking.
Readiness score: shows how recovered you are each morning.
Enterprise controls: team workspaces, brand kits, approvals, single sign-on and security certifications.
Healthspan and medical features: pace of ageing estimate, FDA-cleared ECG and Blood Pressure Insights on top tiers.
Fast delivery with live tracking: shows food preparation and rider location until it reaches you.

scenes.win: Good call. The top-priced plan. It funds the business and is what the brand is known for.
scenes.lose: Users shrug. That feature belongs to a different kind of product. Hint: Cult.fit's promise is "You do not have to commit to one gym or one type of workout."

scenes.title: Make money
scenes.prompt: Investors ask: where will most of Cult.fit's money come from?
right: Memberships (fitness services): ELITE, PRO and centre-only passes.

wrong.text: Accessories: bands, clothing with sensor pockets and chargers.
Contact lenses: own and partner brands.
Commercial and refurbished: machines for hotels, gyms and used equipment sales.
Enterprise contracts: banks, insurers and fintechs pay for voice agents, sales tools and work agents, often with setup help.
Advanced Labs: paid blood test analysis.
Business plan seats with AI: about $20 per member per month (yearly).

scenes.win: That's it. Cult.fit makes money mainly from membership fees (about 70% of revenue) and from selling Cultsport products (about 30%).
scenes.lose: Revenue barely moves, and runway shrinks. Hint, look at how Cult.fit prices things: "Not fixed public pricing. Prices change by city, plan length and sale. As a rough guide, a 12-month ELITE pass in a metro has often sold..."

cursor.section: AI tools for creating and building
cursor.summary: Cursor is a code editor, the app programmers type code into, with AI built in everywhere.
lessons: Product-led growth works when the product gives value in minutes.
If your main cost is a supplier who is also your rival, build your own option (Composer) early.
Pricing is part of the product. Sudden changes can undo years of goodwill.

scenes.title: Who is it for?
scenes.prompt: Day 1. You are the new PM of Cursor. An AI code editor that writes, edits and fixes code with you, now owned by SpaceX after a $60 billion deal in 2026. Who do you build for first?
right: Startup engineer: a full-stack developer at a Bengaluru startup shipping features daily, paying for Cursor from their own pocket or the...

wrong.text: Bank product leader: works at Lloyds and wants a strong digital wallet for its customers.
Enterprise IT buyer: head of digital workplace at a large company in Mumbai or London deciding whether to buy 10,000 Copilot seats.
Working couple in a metro: two professionals in Bengaluru or Gurugram who cook non-veg on weekends and want no butcher trips.
Business traveller: a consultant who books 20 hotel nights a year.
Casual learner: a 25-year-old in Mumbai learning Spanish or Japanese for fun, five minutes before bed.
Local business owner: a restaurant or clinic owner in Pune.

scenes.win: Right. A full-stack developer at a Bengaluru startup shipping features daily, paying for Cursor from their own pocket or the company card. They want: ship features faster; understand an unfamiliar codebase.
scenes.lose: You built for the wrong crowd. They try Cursor once and leave. Hint: Cursor's real users want things like "ship features faster".

scenes.title: What hurts?
scenes.prompt: You sit with a few of these users. Which problem do they keep bringing up?
right: Writing repetitive code and tests takes a lot of a developer's day.

wrong.text: Food is expensive, especially treats and fresh bakery items.
Contactless cards have a £100 limit in the UK.
Every team works differently.
Selling your old car is a separate hassle.
Institutions need safe, regulated custody.
Hotels across Asia are hard to compare in one place.

scenes.win: Yes. Cursor solves it like this: Tab and Agent write most of the routine code for review.
scenes.lose: You fixed a problem these users rarely have. Hint: one thing that frustrates them is "usage runs out before the month ends".

scenes.title: Build the core
scenes.prompt: You can build one thing first. Which feature becomes the heart of Cursor?
right: Tab: predicts the next edit, even across lines, as you type.

wrong.text: AI dubbing and translation: translates scripts and voices into 140+ languages.
Vidyapeeth and Pathshala centres: offline and hybrid classrooms in 353 locations.
Watermarks and provenance labels: marked every video as AI-made.
M-Now 30-minute delivery: thousands of top-selling styles stocked in city stores, delivered in about 30 minutes.
Remix: change any video in the feed with a new prompt.
Reward Partners: swap vouchers for up to 2x value at partners.

scenes.win: Good call. Used many times a minute; this daily habit is what made Cursor loved.
scenes.lose: Users shrug. That feature belongs to a different kind of product. Hint: Cursor's promise is "Write and change code several times faster, inside an editor that already feels familiar."

scenes.title: Make money
scenes.prompt: Investors ask: where will most of Cursor's money come from?

wrong.text: Enterprise plan: higher price for admin, security and APIs.

scenes.win: That's it. Cursor makes money from monthly subscriptions for individuals and per-seat plans for teams and enterprises, plus extra charges for heavy model use.

github-copilot.summary: GitHub Copilot is an AI helper for programmers.
lessons: Being first is not enough. Copilot started the category, but Cursor won many fans by moving faster.

Pricing must match costs. Agent features cost more to run, so GitHub had to add usage limits, which upset users.

gocardless.summary: GoCardless helps businesses collect money directly from their customers' bank accounts.
lessons: Boring infrastructure can be a strong business if it saves customers money every month.
Switching costs, like moving mandates, create loyalty.
Growth at any cost hurt the valuation; profitability came late and the company was sold below its peak.

Trend-led young woman: 17 to 25, follows TikTok and Instagram trends, wants new outfits often.
Trading card collector: 25 to 45, buys and sells Pokemon or sports cards every week, spends thousands a year.
Product manager: plans sprints, writes tickets and reports progress.
The budget viewer on the ad plan: a student in Mexico City or London on the ad-supported plan.

scenes.win: Right. Runs billing at a SaaS company, gym chain or membership business. They want: lower payment fees; fewer failed payments.
scenes.lose: You built for the wrong crowd. They try GoCardless once and leave. Hint: GoCardless's real users want things like "lower payment fees".

scenes.lose: You fixed a problem these users rarely have. Hint: one thing that frustrates them is "card fees of 1.5% to 3%".

scenes.lose: Users shrug. That feature belongs to a different kind of product. Hint: GoCardless's promise is "Collect recurring payments cheaply and reliably, without card expiry, high card fees or chasing customers."

scenes.title: Make money

lyft.summary: Lyft is an app that gets you a car ride.
lessons: Being number two means you cannot win on scale, so pick the customers and features where you can be clearly better, like Lyft did with safety and partner rewards.
In a two-sided marketplace you must keep both sides happy at once; a driver pay cut shows up later as longer rider wait times.
Thin margins mean small changes in insurance or discounts decide profit, so PMs must know the cost of every feature.

Family holiday planner: a parent in Pune planning a Kerala or Dubai trip for four people.
Small-town family traveller: family in a tier-3 town taking a train or bus to a wedding or pilgrimage.

scenes.win: Right. A 28-year-old homemaker in Gorakhpur who buys clothes and kitchen items for the family. They want: get a ₹250 kurti that looks like the ₹800 one in the local market; shop in Hindi without needing an English-speaking app.
scenes.lose: You built for the wrong crowd. They try Meesho once and leave. Hint: Meesho's real users want things like "get a ₹250 kurti that looks like the ₹800 one in the local market".

scenes.lose: You fixed a problem these users rarely have. Hint: one thing that frustrates them is "product looks different from the photo".

google-meet.summary: Google Meet lets you start a video call from a link.
lessons: Distribution can beat features. Meet won share because Calendar adds its link to every invite, not because it was the best video app.

Bundling raises prices for everyone.

krutrim.summary: Krutrim was started in 2023 by Bhavish Aggarwal, who also runs Ola and Ola Electric.
lessons: A big mission ('build India's AI') is not a product.
Competing with free global assistants for consumers needs far better quality, not just local branding.
Pivoting to what customers pay for (computing) can save a company, but it changes what you are.

scenes.title: Who is it for?
scenes.prompt: Day 1. You are the new PM of Krutrim. Ola founder Bhavish Aggarwal's AI company, which set out to build Indian AI models and chips and has pivoted to renting AI computing as a cloud. Who do you build for first?
right: Indian startup developer: a backend engineer at a fintech startup in Bengaluru who needs cheap GPUs and AI models with data kept in India.

wrong.text: Tata Neu loyalist: someone who uses Tata Neu, Croma and Tata cards and wants rewards across them.
The independent artist: an indie musician in Mumbai who releases songs through a distributor.
Brand marketer: a social media manager for a consumer brand.
Small used-car dealer: a dealer in a tier-2 city who needs steady stock to resell.
Frequent traveller: travels for work or holidays several times a year and hates foreign card fees.
Family top-up shopper: parent who needs milk or nappies fast.

scenes.win: Right. A backend engineer at a fintech startup in Bengaluru who needs cheap GPUs and AI models with data kept in India. They want: low cost per AI call; data stored in India for compliance.
scenes.lose: You built for the wrong crowd. They try Krutrim once and leave. Hint: Krutrim's real users want things like "low cost per AI call".

scenes.title: What hurts?
scenes.prompt: You sit with a few of these users. Which problem do they keep bringing up?
right: Indian companies need AI computing with data kept inside India.

wrong.text: Forgot an ingredient while cooking
Charging on long trips is unreliable with other networks.
High brokerage fees at old brokers.
Short trips by car are slow and costly in traffic.
Shopping feels boring.
Games are expensive.

scenes.win: Yes. Krutrim solves it like this: Krutrim Cloud runs in Indian data centres.
scenes.lose: You fixed a problem these users rarely have. Hint: one thing that frustrates them is "worries Krutrim may change direction again".

scenes.title: Build the core
scenes.prompt: You can build one thing first. Which feature becomes the heart of Krutrim?
right: Krutrim Cloud GPUs: rents GPU computing to train and run AI models.

wrong.text: Discovery feed and search: shows trending and recommended characters, with chat counts.
Tab: predicts the next edit, even across lines, as you type.
Low-price API: pay-per-token access to V4-Pro and V4-Flash, with cheaper rates for cached input and off-peak hours.
Star Seller and reviews: badges for sellers with fast shipping, good messages and high ratings.
Business AI on WhatsApp: lets businesses run AI agents that answer customers in WhatsApp chats.
Smart Rules: picks the card automatically by amount, shop or time.

scenes.win: Good call. This is now Krutrim's main business and source of revenue.
scenes.lose: Users shrug. That feature belongs to a different kind of product. Hint: Krutrim's promise is "AI computing and models hosted in India, priced in rupees, with Indian language support, for companies that want local data..."

scenes.title: Make money
scenes.prompt: Investors ask: where will most of Krutrim's money come from?
right: GPU cloud rental: companies pay per hour or reserve GPUs for months.

wrong.text: API (La Plateforme): Pay per million tokens for each model.
Product sales on its app and website: over ₹1,000 crore in FY26; the main source of money.
Compute: selling capacity on Mistral Compute data centres, newer and growing.
Reels ads: ads between short videos, the fastest growing slot.
Commerce: shopping is a top Muse activity, which can bring fees or ads from merchants.
Job seeker services: profile boosts, resume writing, AI tools.

scenes.win: That's it. Krutrim now makes money by renting AI computing (GPUs) and hosted AI models to businesses, billed in rupees.
scenes.lose: Revenue barely moves, and runway shrinks. Hint, look at how Krutrim prices things: "Pay-as-you-go GPU and model pricing in rupees on Krutrim Cloud; enterprise pricing not public."

ondc.summary: On Amazon or Swiggy, the buyer, the seller and the delivery all live inside one company's app.
lessons: An open network needs a great experience on top.
Subsidies can create fake growth.
The UPI comparison has limits: payments are one simple action, but shopping has stock, delivery, returns and support.

scenes.title: Who is it for?
scenes.prompt: Day 1. You are the new PM of ONDC. A government-backed open network that lets any shopping app show products from any seller app, like UPI did for payments. Who do you build for first?
right: Small local shop or restaurant: a neighbourhood store or eatery that finds Swiggy, Zomato or Amazon fees too high.

wrong.text: Parent choosing offline coaching: a parent in a mid-sized city who wants a classroom and discipline for their child.
Upgrading seller: a family selling a 6-year-old Swift to buy a new SUV.
Enterprise self-hoster: an IT head at a bank or telecom who wants an open model to run inside their own data centre for privacy.
Small-town family: a family in Nashik buying glasses for kids and parents.
Homeowner thinking of selling: a family checking what their home is worth.
Weekend moviegoer: a 25-year-old office worker in Bengaluru who watches one or two films a month with friends.

scenes.win: Right. A neighbourhood store or eatery that finds Swiggy, Zomato or Amazon fees too high. They want: sell online without paying 25 to 30% commission; keep control of customer and pricing.
scenes.lose: You built for the wrong crowd. They try ONDC once and leave. Hint: ONDC's real users want things like "sell online without paying 25 to 30% commission".

scenes.title: What hurts?
scenes.prompt: You sit with a few of these users. Which problem do they keep bringing up?
right: Big marketplaces charge sellers 25 to 40% commission.

wrong.text: Most big apps are built for English speakers, so many Indians feel left out.
Institutions need safe, regulated custody.
Loneliness and no one to talk to late at night
Cycle tracking by app logging is unreliable.
Delivery fees add up.
Losing your place between devices.

scenes.win: Yes. ONDC solves it like this: Open network with about 8 to 10% fees and near-zero network fee.
scenes.lose: You fixed a problem these users rarely have. Hint: one thing that frustrates them is "seller apps are hard to set up".

scenes.title: Build the core
scenes.prompt: You can build one thing first. Which feature becomes the heart of ONDC?
right: Open protocol (Beckn): shared technical rules for search, order, pay, track and return.

wrong.text: Sidekick: AI assistant that builds reports, discounts and automations.
Online consultation: Chat or video with a doctor within minutes, with a digital prescription.
Fulfillment and Quick: warehousing and fast local delivery.
Google Play Store: main app store with millions of apps.
Wholesale catalogue: lists FMCG, staples, pharma, fresh produce and electronics at bulk prices.
Style and image references: upload images to copy a style or a character's look.

scenes.win: Good call. Lets any app talk to any other app, which is the whole idea.
scenes.lose: Users shrug. That feature belongs to a different kind of product. Hint: ONDC's promise is "For sellers: reach buyers on many apps without paying high marketplace fees or being locked into one platform."

scenes.title: Make money
scenes.prompt: Investors ask: where will most of ONDC's money come from?
right: Network fees: a small fee per transaction, planned from December 2024 but postponed for retail.

wrong.text: Final value fees: about 13.6% of the total sale price in most US categories, plus about $0.30 to $0.40 per order.
Europe and chauffeur: FreeNow taxi app in Europe and TBR Global Chauffeuring, being rebranded as Alcove in 2027.
Food: premium food in stores and via Ocado, the largest share of sales.
Films, parks and merchandise: the Super Mario Bros.
International and franchise: stores abroad and franchise partners.
Services to insurers: fees for marketing, lead generation, tech and outsourced services.

scenes.win: That's it. ONDC is a non-profit. It aims to cover its costs from small network fees on transactions, but these fees were postponed for most categories and only started in financial services. It has relied on...
scenes.lose: Revenue barely moves, and runway shrinks. Hint, look at how ONDC prices things: "Network fee near zero for most retail."

peloton.summary: Peloton sells an exercise bike or treadmill with a big screen.
lessons: A temporary boom is not a new normal.
Hardware can be a hook for a subscription.
Price rises can raise revenue but also churn.

scenes.title: Who is it for?
scenes.prompt: Day 1. You are the new PM of Peloton. A US company that sells connected exercise bikes, treadmills and rowers plus a monthly membership for live and on-demand classes. Who do you build for first?
right: Busy working parent: a 40-year-old with kids who cannot get to a gym or spin studio.

wrong.text: Quick top-up shopper: a working professional who orders a few items several times a week.
Casual learner: a 25-year-old in Mumbai learning Spanish or Japanese for fun, five minutes before bed.
Credit builder: a 23-year-old with no credit history.
Small bus operator: owner of 15 buses running between Chennai and Madurai.
Sports and event bettor: a 28-year-old who trades event contracts on NFL games and elections.
Product marketing manager: makes product demo and how-to videos at a software company.

scenes.win: Right. A 40-year-old with kids who cannot get to a gym or spin studio. They want: short, effective workouts at home; motivation to stay consistent.
scenes.lose: You built for the wrong crowd. They try Peloton once and leave. Hint: Peloton's real users want things like "short, effective workouts at home".

scenes.title: What hurts?
scenes.prompt: You sit with a few of these users. Which problem do they keep bringing up?
right: No time to go to a gym or studio class.

wrong.text: Fear of fraud when buying from unknown sites.
Hard to build credit.
Minimum balance rules.
AI chatbots make things up and do not show where facts came from.
Smartphones were too expensive for most Indians.
Limited range from local distributors.

scenes.win: Yes. Peloton solves it like this: Classes at home, any time, from 5 minutes to an hour.
scenes.lose: You fixed a problem these users rarely have. Hint: one thing that frustrates them is "membership price rises".

scenes.title: Build the core
scenes.prompt: You can build one thing first. Which feature becomes the heart of Peloton?
right: Live and on-demand classes: thousands of classes across many workout types.

wrong.text: Recovery score: morning score from 0 to 100% showing readiness.
Integrations and workflows: apps, bots and no-code Workflow Builder.
Sleep score: measures sleep time, stages and quality every night.
Co-authoring on OneDrive and SharePoint: several people edit the same file live, with version history.
Strain and Sleep: tracks effort through the day and sleep quality and need at night.
Participant registry: lists approved buyer apps, seller apps and logistics partners.

scenes.win: Good call. The content is what members pay for every month.
scenes.lose: Users shrug. That feature belongs to a different kind of product. Hint: Peloton's promise is "A boutique fitness class experience at home, any time, with motivating instructors and a sense of community, so you actually keep..."

scenes.title: Make money
scenes.prompt: Investors ask: where will most of Peloton's money come from?
right: Subscriptions: All-Access Membership for hardware owners and Peloton App tiers; the majority of revenue.

wrong.text: Corporate plans: companies pay for employee passes through cultpassX.
Prediction markets: $173 million in Q3 2026 from fees on event contracts.
Accessories: bands, clothing with sensor pockets and chargers.
Fans and smart locks: ₹1,158 crore in FY26, segment margin 11.7%.
Teams and enterprise: plans for sports teams, military and companies.
Webinars, Events and Rooms: add-ons for large events and meeting rooms.

scenes.win: That's it. Peloton sells hardware, often at low margin, to lock people into a high-margin monthly membership.
scenes.lose: Revenue barely moves, and runway shrinks. Hint, look at how Peloton prices things: "All-Access Membership is about $44 to $50 a month in the US after the October 2025 price rise; app tiers are cheaper."

scenes.prompt: The team needs one number to chase every week. Which north star fits Peloton?

wrong.text: Active subscribers still on treatment after 6 months
Number of orders delivered and kept (not returned) per month
Completed consultations per month (clinic plus online) rated as satisfactory
Number of homes on smart tariffs saving money and shifting use to cheaper, greener times
Weekly active athletes who upload at least one activity and receive or give kudos
Weekly answered questions where the user does not need to search again elsewhere

scenes.win: Yes. Members who work out regularly get fitter and are far less likely to cancel, which drives membership revenue.
scenes.lose: The team chases the wrong number and the product drifts. Hint: a good north star counts the moment a Peloton user gets real value.

revolut.summary: Revolut is a bank in an app. You get a card, an account and can spend in 150+ currencies with low fees, which made it famous with travellers. Over time it added savings, stock and crypto trading, insurance, eSIMs for travel and business accounts. Most...
lessons: Start with one sharp hook. Cheap FX for travellers brought users in before Revolut added everything else.
Cross-selling builds value. Each extra product raises revenue per user and makes leaving harder.
Regulation is product work. The long wait for a UK licence limited what Revolut could offer.

scenes.title: Who is it for?

scenes.lose: You fixed a problem these users rarely have. Hint: one thing that frustrates them is "weekend FX markups".

truecaller.summary: When an unknown number calls, Truecaller shows the caller's name and warns you if it is spam, like a loan agent or a scammer.
lessons: A product that gets better as more people use it can win a market, but a government rule can still change the game overnight.
Ads on a free app are fragile. Truecaller moved toward subscriptions and business revenue to make income steadier.
Privacy is part of the product. Building a phone book from users' contacts gave Truecaller its edge but also its biggest complaint.

scenes.win: Good call. The core profit engine and the product Zopa is known for.
scenes.lose: Users shrug. That feature belongs to a different kind of product. Hint: Zopa's promise is "Fair, fast credit with a price based on your real risk, and good savings rates, from a bank built only for the app."

scenes.title: Make money

wrong.text: Government UPI incentives: payments from the government to support UPI growth, which change each year.

Subscriptions: individual, student, family and Runna bundle plans; the large majority of revenue.
Possible UPI MDR: if a 0.4% fee on large UPI merchant payments goes live, analysts estimate ₹192 to 461 crore extra yearly revenue.
Network fees: a small fee per transaction, planned from December 2024 but postponed for retail.

scenes.win: That's it. Zopa makes money by lending. It pays savers interest, lends that money at higher rates, and keeps the difference after losses. The current account adds cheaper deposits and better data for lending.
scenes.lose: Revenue barely moves, and runway shrinks. Hint, look at how Zopa prices things: "Personal loan representative APR varies by amount and term, typically in the mid to high single digits for larger loans, higher for small..."
